title: Brothers by nature
hookLine: don't be harsh with your slave; he's your brother, born of the same Zeus (Discourses 1.13)
carry: look where your eyes are pointed

lines: HOW DO I EAT TO PLEASE THE GODS?
LOOK AT WHO BRINGS THE WATER.
cards: The coffee comes out lukewarm. The order is wrong. The person at the counter didn't hear you the first time.

It's amazing how fast a calm, kind person can turn sharp at someone whose job is to serve them. A student once asked Epictetus something that sounds almost silly: how can I eat dinner in a way that pleases the gods?
His answer went straight to the person bringing the hot water.

teach.b: This is Discourses book one, chapter thirteen. Eat justly, Epictetus says, with gratitude, moderation and good order, and you've eaten in a way the gods accept. Then he gets concrete.
You call for warm water, and the slave doesn't hear, or brings it lukewarm, or isn't in the house at all. Not to rage, not to explode: that is acceptable to the gods.
But how am I supposed to put up with someone like that? Here Epictetus turns sharp.

teach.h: YOUR BROTHER, FROM THE SAME SEED.
teach.b: Won't you bear with your own brother, he asks, who has Zeus as his ancestor, born from the same seed as you? You're not his owner first; you're his kin. The student pushes back: but I bought him.
He didn't buy me. And Epictetus says: look where your eyes are pointed. Down at the dirt, at the laws of dead men, not at the laws of the gods.
We should hear this with open eyes. Epictetus had been a slave himself before he was freed, yet this chapter doesn't call for slavery to end. It asks owners for gentleness, not freedom.

But the root of the idea is bigger than its century: whoever hands you the cup is your brother or sister by nature. The week in a breath: kin, not more books, it fits, look closer, love stays, content, and now adelphos.

how: Some readers of Epictetus apply this chapter to how they treat people who serve them, such as waiters, cleaners and call-center staff, especially when something goes wrong.

o: a fellow student of the same teacher
brother: kin, born of the same womb

games.q: brothers by nature: tap the pairs.

s: in this chapter Epictetus calls for slaves to be set free
he doesn't; he asks owners for gentleness, which is why we read it with open eyes.
Epictetus was himself enslaved before being freed
he was owned by a powerful freedman at Nero's court.
Epictetus says the servant shares the same divine origin as the master
born from the same seed, with Zeus as ancestor.

games.q: you're a Roman master. you asked for warm water and the slave brought it lukewarm. what does Epictetus say?
o: punish him so it doesn't happen again.
bear with your brother; he comes from the same seed as you.
games.why: he calls the servant the master's brother by nature, and says looking only at 'I bought him' is looking at the laws of dead men.

practice: Bring to mind the people who served you this week: a cashier, a driver, a nurse, a cleaner, someone on a customer service line.
Picture one face, even one you barely saw, and let yourself see them as kin, with a family, a tired back, a whole life.
If you were short with anyone, notice it without beating yourself up, and let one gentle word for the next person come to mind.

wordCard.voice: Adelphos. Greek for brother, literally 'from the same womb': Epictetus' word for the one who serves you, your kin before anything else.

orig.note: Greek adelphos: brother, literally 'from the same womb'; Epictetus uses it for the master's kinship with the slave.

carryVoice: Your line: look where your eyes are pointed. Up, toward kin, not down at the dirt. A week done.

sources.ref: Discourses 1.13 (how everything may be done acceptably to the gods)
